description: We are freshman university students based in San Francisco. First time participating in a Hackathon!
summary:
HARK! NASA is a web page that turns NASA’s animation of global sea surface temperature and currents into live orchestral music. NASA’s Earth Information Center shows Earth science almost entirely through color, which shuts out people who are blind, have low vision, or are color blind. Our project answers the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by pairing a NASA visualization with sound generated in real time in the browser.
Temperature sets the pitch of the melody: piano plays cold water, and brass plays hot water. Strings play the currents and swell as the flow gets stronger. Listeners explore the map with hand gestures read by a webcam, with voice commands, or with a mouse, touchscreen, or keyboard, and every reading can be spoken aloud, so the screen is optional. It matters because sound gives everyone a second way to notice patterns in the ocean, and gives people who cannot read a color bar a first way.
details:
What it does. HARK! NASA plays the ocean as an orchestra. You load NASA’s Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature animation, or use the built-in sample map, and the page turns what is on screen into music while the video plays. You can point at one place and hear it, zoom into a region, ask “Where am I?”, or sweep a scan across the whole map that plays one note per strip.

How it works. The page matches the color of each ocean pixel to NASA’s 0 to 32 °C color bar to recover a temperature, and skips land. It reads the currents from how the streaks move between video frames. Those readings drive the instruments: melody pitch rises with temperature on a pentatonic scale, piano plays cold water, brass plays hot water, and strings play the currents with more vibrato and volume as the flow strengthens. Steady flow sounds smooth and uneven flow sounds detached. East or west flow moves the sound between the ears, and north or south flow steps the melody up or down.

How people use it. A webcam reads hand gestures: one finger points, two fingers zoom in, three zoom out, four fingers ask for a reading or set the scan direction, a fist starts a scan and two hands stop it. Voice commands such as “go to the Gulf Stream” do the same, as do a mouse, touch and the keyboard. Readings are spoken aloud. Camera video is processed on the user’s own computer and never leaves it.

Benefits and intended impact. It opens a color-only NASA visualization to people who are blind, have low vision, or are color blind, and gives every listener a new way to notice patterns. It is free, runs in a browser and needs nothing installed.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page; the Web Audio API for sound; MediaPipe Hands for gesture tracking; the browser’s speech recognition and speech synthesis; GitHub Pages for hosting.

How it is creative. Each signal in the data gets its own instrument family, so temperature and currents can be heard at the same time, and the listener plays the ocean by hand like an instrument.

What we considered. Sonification research shows listeners tend to hear higher pitch as “more”, so warmer water sounds higher. Human hearing is harshest at about 2 to 5 kHz, so the melody stays below that and the volume starts low. A direct pixel-to-sound translation was noisy, so notes snap to a musical scale. We have not yet run listening tests; our report sets out four hypotheses and a test plan, and we make no claims about blind users until they have tried it. Full report: https://shorturl.at/Waehs
